reviewMetadata.sourceLessonFamily: Advanced Trigonometry: Unit Circle and Identities

learnerMaterial.title: Derive Unit-Circle Symmetry Identities
learnerMaterial.subject: mathematics
learnerMaterial.lessonGoal: Use unit-circle coordinates and transformations to derive trigonometric symmetry and periodicity identities.
successCriteria: I connect cosine and sine to x- and y-coordinates.
I derive signs from a geometric transformation rather than memorizing a quadrant rule.
keyPoints: The point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ).
Reflections and rotations determine how coordinates change.
A full 2π rotation returns to the same point.

vocabulary.definition: repeating after a fixed input interval
an equality derived from a geometric symmetry of the unit circle

rows: π − θ | reflect across y-axis | (−cos θ, sin θ)
θ + 2π | full rotation | (cos θ, sin θ)

sections.title: Worked example: derive sin(π − θ)
sections.directions: The identity is derived from coordinates on this page.

items.prompt: Derive sin(π − θ) and cos(π − θ).

steps: The point at θ is (cos θ, sin θ).
The angle π − θ reflects that point across the y-axis.
Therefore the new point is (−cos θ, sin θ).
So cos(π − θ) = −cos θ and sin(π − θ) = sin θ.

items.prompt: Which transformation takes the point for θ to the point for −θ?

feedback.correct: That reflection preserves the x-coordinate and negates the y-coordinate.
feedback.incorrect: Compare (cos θ, sin θ) with (cos θ, −sin θ) and identify which axis reflection has that effect.

items.prompt: Derive sin(−θ) and cos(−θ) from the unit-circle reflection across the x-axis.

feedback.correct: Your coordinate transformation establishes sine's odd behavior and cosine's even behavior.
feedback.incorrect: Write the original coordinate pair, apply (x,y) → (x,−y), then read cosine and sine from the result.

items.prompt: Explain why sin(θ + 2π) = sin θ and cos(θ + 2π) = cos θ without citing a memorized formula.

feedback.correct: You connected a full rotation to the same terminal point and therefore the same coordinates.
feedback.incorrect: Describe where a 2π rotation sends the terminal point on the unit circle.

sections.title: Reteach: use a coordinate-change ledger
sections.body: For each move, record x: same or negated; y: same or negated. Then translate x to cosine and y to sine.

items.prompt: A rotation by π sends (x,y) to (−x,−y). Use that fact to state sin(θ + π) and cos(θ + π).

feedback.correct: Your ledger negated both coordinates under a half-turn.
feedback.incorrect: Replace x with cos θ and y with sin θ after applying (x,y) → (−x,−y).

items.prompt: Derive the sine and cosine identities for 2π − θ. Name the unit-circle transformation, show the coordinate change, and state both identities.

feedback.correct: Your transformation, coordinates, and identities form one coherent derivation.
feedback.incorrect: Locate 2π − θ as the reflection of θ across the x-axis, then track x and y separately.

whatYouLearned: Reflections explain sign changes in sine and cosine.
Periodicity follows from returning to the same point after a full rotation.
